questions.q: According to the chapter, how is science best described?
o: A process: a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity and asks questions
A fixed list of facts to be learnt by heart
A subject that can be done only inside a laboratory
A set of answers that never change
questions.a: A process: a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity, asks questions and is open to the unknown.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the 'deeper questions' the chapter says we will try to ask in Grade 7?
o: Why do events happen the way they do?
How many chapters does this book have?
What is the name of this textbook?
Which chapter of the book comes first?
questions.a: Why do events happen the way they do? (The other deeper questions are How do things work? and What can we learn from the patterns that we see in nature?)

questions.q: According to the chapter, what does each chapter of the Grade 7 book build on?
o: What you already know
What scientists in laboratories have already proved
The answers given at the end of the book
The chapter that comes just after it
questions.a: What you already know: each chapter builds on what you already know and encourages you to ask questions, explore and think like a scientist.

questions.q: Ravi says science is only about very big things such as the Sun and the stars. Which example from the chapter shows that science also covers very small things?
o: Looking at tiny cells inside a leaf
Studying the movement of the sun and the stars
Studying the melting of a glacier
Studying the Earth casting a shadow
questions.a: Looking at tiny cells inside a leaf; the chapter says the world of science covers everything, small and large, near and far.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter says science is not just about discovery but also about responsibility.
Reason (R): The chapter says human activities are linked to what happens in the natural world.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because our activities affect the natural world, studying science brings a responsibility towards it.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter.
Statement I: The chapters of the book look different, but they are all interconnected.
Statement II: Once an experiment confirms what we expected, there are no more questions to ask about it.
Statement III: Scientific ideas in one area can allow us to ask questions in another area.
Which of the statements match the chapter?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
All three
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the chapter says even experiments that seem to confirm what we think might lead to more questions and more experiments.

questions.q: A class watches a paper plane glide across the room and an eagle soar outside. Which statement matches the chapter's account of how humans came to fly?
o: The dream of flying started with simple observations and experiments, from studying bird wings to designing aircraft.
Aircraft were designed first, and people studied bird wings only afterwards.
Flight was understood without any experiments, just by reading about it.
Only modern engineers have ever studied flight; early inventors did not.
questions.a: The dream of flying started with simple observations and experiments: from early inventors studying bird wings to modern engineers designing aircraft.

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the idea of the chapter in Column II.
Column I: 1. Noticing that ants walk in a line to the kitchen every evening and asking why  2. Seeing that waste dumped near a pond makes its water smell  3. Using a hand lens to look at a leaf  4. Asking how a ceiling fan works
Column II: A. Science covers things small and large  B. How do things work?  C. What can we learn from patterns in nature?  D. Human activities are linked to the natural world
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B: the ants show a pattern in nature; the smelly pond links a human activity to nature; the leaf under a lens shows science covers small things; the fan asks how things work.

questions.q: The chapter says the book is not just a textbook with facts but an invitation. State any two things it invites you to do.
questions.a: Any two of: to question; to perform experiments; to explore.
s: First thing the book invites you to do (question / perform experiments / explore)
Second, different thing from the same list

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says the world of science covers only the things that are near us. Give the verdict and correct the statement if needed.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the world of science covers everything, small and large, near and far; for example, the movement of the sun and the stars, or how water flows underground.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: science covers everything, small and large, near and far (e.g. the movement of the sun and the stars)

questions.q:
(a) Besides making simple observations and doing fun experiments, what else does the chapter say you will do in the chapters that follow?
(b) Complete the chapter's line: each chapter encourages you to ask questions, explore, do hands-on experiments, and think like a ...
questions.a: (a) Dive into topics that need careful thinking. (b) ... scientist.
s: (a) dive into topics that need careful thinking
(b) a scientist

questions.q:
(a) Complete the saying the chapter recalls from Grade 6: 'To be a wise person, you must be a ...'
(b) According to the chapter, what do great scientists do besides answering questions?
questions.a: (a) '... whys person'. (b) They ask amazing questions.
s: (a) 'a whys person'
(b) they ask amazing (interesting) questions

questions.q:
Mohan says, 'I only like physics, so a discovery in biology can never matter to me.'
(a) What does the chapter say about the different fields of science in the book?
(b) Use it to reply to Mohan.
questions.a: (a) Physics, chemistry, biology and earth sciences may appear as different chapters, but they are all interconnected. (b) Ideas in one area often inspire discoveries in another, or at least let us ask questions in another, so a biology discovery can give Mohan new questions in physics.
s: (a) the fields are all interconnected
(b) an idea in one area can inspire a discovery or new questions in another, so it can matter to him

questions.q:
Ishaan's group expected a heavy steel ball to roll down a slope much faster than a light glass marble. In their test, both reached the bottom at about the same time. Ishaan wants to rub the result out because it 'does not fit'.
(a) How does the chapter describe science as a way of thinking?
(b) Use this to advise Ishaan what to do with his result.
questions.a: (a) Science is a process, a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity, asks questions and is open to the unknown. (b) He should not rub it out: an unexpected result is exactly what an open, curious way of thinking welcomes. He should record it, ask why it happened and test again.
s: (a) a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity, asks questions and is open to the unknown
(b) keep and record the unexpected result, ask why and test again, because science is open to the unknown

questions.q: The chapter says the world of science covers everything, 'small and large, near and far'. Give three examples the chapter uses to show this.
questions.a: Any three of: tiny cells inside a leaf; the movement of the sun and the stars; testing the materials around us at home; how water flows underground.
s: First example from the chapter
Second example from the chapter
Third example from the chapter

questions.q: Claim: 'Discoveries are made only by scientists in laboratories. A Class 7 student cannot make any discovery.' Is the claim right? Use the chapter to give your verdict and two reasons.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the book will help you become an explorer, making small discoveries for yourself. It also asks students to step out of the book and the classroom and experience the world through activities and experiments, which are stepping stones to deeper understanding.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Reason 1: the book helps you become an explorer making small discoveries for yourself
Reason 2: students step out of the classroom and learn through activities and experiments

questions.q: Every summer, the water from the hand pump in Ritu's colony drops lower, while more houses dig borewells each year. Using the chapter, show in three linked steps how a young science explorer would move from noticing this to acting responsibly.
questions.a: Step 1: notice and ask a deeper question, such as why the water drops every summer or what pattern it follows. Step 2: see the link the chapter describes between human activities (more borewells, more water drawn) and what happens in the natural world (less water underground). Step 3: use science to address the challenge, such as suggesting ways to save or recharge water, because the chapter says science can help create a more sustainable world.
s: Asks a deeper question (why / what pattern) about the falling water
Links a human activity to the change in nature, as the chapter says activities are linked to the natural world
Proposes a responsible action, using the chapter's idea that science can help create a sustainable world

questions.q:
Leela is making a science-fair poster called 'From a paper plane to an aircraft' to explain the opening page of the chapter.
(a) What does the chapter say a paper plane inspired?
(b) Name the two groups of people the chapter mentions in the story of flight.
(c) What does the chapter say the dream of flying started with?
(d) Her partner wants the poster's headline to be 'Aircraft were made by experts; curiosity about simple things did not matter.' Using your answers to (a)-(c), decide whether this headline fits the chapter and justify your decision.
questions.a: (a) Real scientific explorations of flight. (b) Early inventors studying bird wings, and modern engineers designing aircraft. (c) Simple observations and experiments. (d) It does not fit: (a) shows a simple paper plane inspired real exploration, (b) shows the work began with inventors studying something as ordinary as bird wings before engineers designed aircraft, and (c) shows the dream started with simple observations, so curiosity about simple things led the way.
s: (a) real scientific explorations of flight
(b) early inventors studying bird wings and modern engineers designing aircraft
(c) simple observations and experiments
(d) decides the headline does not fit, using at least two of (a)-(c) to show simple curiosity led to aircraft

questions.q: The chapter is called 'The Ever-Evolving World of Science'. Justify this title with five different ideas from the chapter, one mark each.
questions.a: Any five of: science is a process, a way of thinking, not only facts; science is an ongoing process of discovery; even experiments that confirm what we think can lead to more questions and more experiments; ideas in one area inspire discoveries or questions in another; each chapter builds on what you already know, and Grade 7 asks deeper questions than Grade 6; the dream of flying grew from simple observations to modern aircraft; science welcomes curiosity and is open to the unknown.
s: One valid idea from the list
A second, different valid idea
A third, different valid idea
A fourth, different valid idea
A fifth, different valid idea

questions.q:
Class 7A in Indore kept a 'Question Box' for four weeks. Each Friday the teacher counted all the questions and the 'deeper' ones (how something works, why an event happens, or what pattern is seen in nature).
Week 1: 20 questions, 8 deeper. Week 2: 16 questions, 8 deeper. Week 3: 12 questions, 9 deeper. Week 4: 10 questions, 8 deeper.
(a) How many questions, and how many deeper questions, were put in the box in all four weeks?
(b) What percentage of each week's questions were deeper, and which week had the highest percentage?
(c) Describe how the number of questions and the share of deeper questions changed from Week 1 to Week 4.
(d) The teacher can praise only one week at assembly: Week 1 or Week 4. Decide which, and justify using one idea from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 20 + 16 + 12 + 10 = 58 questions; 8 + 8 + 9 + 8 = 33 deeper. (b) Week 1: 40%, Week 2: 50%, Week 3: 75%, Week 4: 80%; Week 4 is highest. (c) The number of questions fell from 20 to 10, but the share of deeper questions rose from 40% to 80%. (d) Either, if justified: Week 4, because the chapter wants deeper Grade 7 questions (how, why, patterns); or Week 1, because the chapter says science welcomes curiosity and asking many interesting questions is what great scientists do.
s: (a) 58 questions in all and 33 deeper
(c) total fell (20 to 10) while the share of deeper questions rose (40% to 80%)
(d) a decision supported by a chapter idea (deeper questions, or welcoming curiosity) and the data

questions.q: The chapter's tour begins with the properties of materials around us. How does the chapter describe these materials?
o: Things we experience but perhaps never ask questions about
Things we can see only through a microscope
Things found only inside a science laboratory
Things that are far away in space
questions.a: Mostly the things we experience but perhaps never ask questions about.

questions.q: The chapter says some changes can be reversed and others cannot. Which pair from the chapter's list of changes has one change that can be reversed and one that cannot?
o: Ice melting into water, and a torch battery running out
A torch battery running out, and fruits ripening
Fruits ripening, and rocks breaking into pebbles
Rocks breaking into pebbles, and a torch battery running out
questions.a: Ice melting into water, and a torch battery running out: the water can be frozen back into ice, but the chapter says a run-out torch battery can't be used again. In each of the other pairs, neither change can be undone.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what does the heat from the Sun do to the water in the seas?
o: It makes the water evaporate
It makes the water freeze
It turns the water into salt
It pushes the water straight into the ground
questions.a: It makes the water evaporate; the water later falls as rain.

questions.q: Which list contains ONLY changes that the chapter names?
o: Batteries running out, fruits ripening, rocks breaking into pebbles
Batteries running out, a lamp glowing, the Sun rising
Fruits ripening, cells in a leaf, shadows of objects
Ice melting, the Moon going around the Earth, a sour fruit
questions.a: Batteries running out, fruits ripening, rocks breaking into pebbles (the chapter also names ice melting into water).

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter's work with batteries, lamps and wires takes us into the world of metals and non-metals.
Reason (R): Asking what kind of materials we need to make a lamp glow leads to classifying materials based on their properties.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the lamp-glow question leads to classifying materials by their properties, and that classification is what takes us into metals and non-metals.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter's tour.
Statement I: The chapter says water is everywhere.
Statement II: The chapter says questions such as why some fruits are sour are about things we experience but perhaps never ask questions about.
Statement III: The chapter says the topics of the book come only from physics.
Which of the statements are correct?
o: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
All three
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: the chapter says the topics come from different fields of science, from physics and chemistry to biology and earth sciences.

questions.q: The chapter lists these changes: 'batteries run out, ice melts into water, fruits ripen, rocks break into pebbles'. Rekha wants to add one more. Which of her observations is another change in a material, like the items in this list?
o: A piece of wood burns and turns into ash
A steel spoon is harder than a plastic spoon
A copper wire is shiny and bends easily
A stone lies still on the road all day
questions.a: A piece of wood burning into ash: like the items in the list, the material itself changes. The spoon and the copper wire describe properties of materials, and a stone lying still shows no change at all.

questions.q: Arjun melts an ice cube into water in a steel bowl, then puts the bowl in the freezer and gets an ice cube back. Which idea from the chapter's tour does this show?
o: Some changes can be reversed
No change can ever be reversed
Changes happen only in metals
Materials can be classified as metals and non-metals
questions.a: Some changes can be reversed: the water turned back into ice. (The chapter says some changes can be reversed and others cannot.)

questions.q: The chapter says we will explore the kinds of changes that happen around us. Into which two kinds does it divide these changes?
questions.a: Changes that can be reversed, and changes that cannot be reversed.
s: Changes that can be reversed
Changes that cannot be reversed

questions.q: True or False: According to the chapter, a torch battery that has run out can be used again. Give the verdict and correct the statement if needed.
questions.a: False. The chapter says a torch battery runs out eventually and can't be used again.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a torch battery runs out eventually and cannot be used again

questions.q:
(a) Name the three things the chapter says we will play with to find other kinds of properties of materials.
(b) What question about a lamp does the chapter ask?
questions.a: (a) Electric batteries, lamps and wires. (b) What kind of materials do we need to make a lamp glow?
s: (a) batteries, lamps and wires
(b) what kind of materials do we need to make a lamp glow

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says that some changes in water are hidden changes that we do not see. Give the verdict and say which changes the chapter sets them against.
questions.a: True. The chapter speaks of the hidden changes in water that we do not see, and sets them against the changes in materials around us that we do see.
s: Verdict: True
Set against: the changes in materials around us that we see

questions.q:
Rohan says, 'Fruits ripening and rocks breaking into pebbles have nothing in common.'
(a) Under which topic does the chapter place both of them?
(b) Name one more example the chapter puts in the same list.
questions.a: (a) Changes that happen around us. (b) Batteries running out, or ice melting into water.
s: (a) changes that happen around us
(b) batteries running out / ice melting into water

questions.q:
The chapter gives two examples of how heat flows: an ice cube melting in a glass and a glacier melting.
(a) What is common to both examples?
(b) How are the two examples different in size and place?
questions.a: (a) In both, ice melts because heat flows into it. (b) The ice cube is small and close by, in a glass at home; the glacier is huge and far away, showing that science covers small and large, near and far.
s: (a) both are ice melting as heat flows into it
(b) ice cube small and near, glacier large and far

questions.q:
Answer from the start of the chapter's tour of the book.
(a) Name any two of the fields of science the chapter says the book's topics come from.
(b) What does the chapter say the tour will start by looking at?
(c) Complete the chapter's sentence that begins the journey of water: 'Water is, of course, ...'
questions.a: (a) Any two of: physics, chemistry, biology, earth sciences. (b) The properties of materials around us. (c) '... everywhere'.
s: (a) any two of physics, chemistry, biology, earth sciences
(b) the properties of materials around us
(c) everywhere

questions.q: Claim: 'Science can study only the changes we can see happening in front of us.' Does the chapter's tour support this claim? Give your verdict and two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter speaks of 'the hidden changes in water that we do not see', separate from the changes in materials we see. For example, water evaporates from the seas with the heat from the Sun, and rain may trickle down into the ground somewhere far away; we do not watch these, yet the book studies them.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong / not supported
Reason 1: the chapter mentions hidden changes in water that we do not see
Reason 2: an example, such as evaporation from the seas or rain trickling into the ground far away

questions.q:
Mira's mother sets curd from milk in the same kitchen all year. In summer the curd sets in 6 hours; in winter it takes 10 hours. One winter night she sets the curd at 9 p.m. and wants it ready for breakfast at 6 a.m.
(a) Which line of the chapter explains why the curd sets faster in summer?
(b) Will the curd be ready at 6 a.m.? Show your working.
(c) Suggest one change she could make so it is ready in time, and say why it works.
questions.a: (a) Some changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated; the warmer summer kitchen makes the curd set faster. (b) From 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. is 9 hours, but winter curd needs 10 hours, so it will not be ready; it will be 1 hour short. (c) Either set it by 8 p.m. (6 a.m. minus 10 hours), or keep the pot in a warmer place, such as near the stove, because the change happens faster when it is warmer.
s: (a) some changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated
(b) 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. is 9 hours, less than 10 hours, so not ready (1 hour short)
(c) a workable change (set it by 8 p.m., or keep it warmer) with the reason

questions.q:
Class 7 in Nellore filled the same steel bowl with 1 litre of water and kept it on the open terrace for 3 days in January, and again for 3 days in May. In January the bowl lost 45 mL; in May it lost 120 mL.
(a) Find how much water the bowl lost per day in each month.
(b) In which month did it lose water faster, and which line of the chapter explains it?
(c) Where does the chapter say this water goes next?
(d) At the May rate, how much water would the bowl lose in 5 days?
questions.a: (a) January: 45 / 3 = 15 mL per day; May: 120 / 3 = 40 mL per day. (b) In May, the hotter month; the chapter says that with the heat from the Sun, water evaporates. (c) It falls as rain, perhaps trickling down into the ground somewhere far away. (d) 40 x 5 = 200 mL.
s: (a) 15 mL per day in January and 40 mL per day in May
(b) May, because heat from the Sun makes water evaporate
(c) it falls as rain and may trickle into the ground far away

questions.a: (i) Properties of materials around us: like the chapter's question 'why are some fruits sour?', it is about things we experience but never ask about. (ii) The journey of water: with the heat from the Sun, water evaporates. (iii) Properties of materials found with batteries, lamps and wires: what materials make a lamp glow leads to classifying them as metals and non-metals. (iv) Heat: either 'some changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated' or 'how heat flows' (heat flows from the flame into the wax); both are accepted. (v) Changes around us: like batteries running out or rocks breaking into pebbles, it is one of the changes that happen around us.
s: (i) properties of materials around us (why are some fruits sour)
(ii) journey of water: heat from the Sun makes water evaporate
(iii) properties of materials leading to metals and non-metals
(iv) either heat link: changes happen or happen faster on heating, or heat flows from the flame into the wax
(v) changes that happen around us

questions.q:
Class 7C at a school in Nashik kept a 'Changes Diary' for one week and wrote one entry each day.
Monday: the ice in the water jug had melted by lunch.
Tuesday: the green bananas in the fruit basket turned yellow and ripe.
Wednesday: the torch in the store room stopped working because its battery had run out.
Thursday: a rock at the edge of the garden had broken into pebbles.
(a) How many entries did the class write?
(b) Which entry is about something the chapter says can't be used again?
(c) Which entry shows fruits ripening?
(d) The chapter studies how heat flows through the melting of ice. Which entry is an example of this?
questions.a: (a) 4 entries. (b) Wednesday: the torch battery that ran out. (c) Tuesday: the bananas ripening. (d) Monday: the ice in the jug melting, like the chapter's ice cube melting in a glass.
s: (a) 4 entries
(b) Wednesday, the battery that ran out
(c) Tuesday, the bananas ripening
(d) Monday, the ice melting

questions.q: According to the chapter, how did early humans tell the time, long before electric clocks and digital watches?
o: From the position of the shadows of objects in the Sun
From the shape of the Moon each night
From the height of water in a pot
From the time birds began to sing
questions.a: They observed the shadows of objects in the Sun and used the position of the shadows to tell the time.

questions.q: What does the chapter say leads to the phenomena of eclipses?
o: The Earth and the Moon casting shadows
Clouds covering the Sun
The Sun stopping its light for a while
The Earth rotating around its axis once a day
questions.a: The Earth and the Moon can cast shadows, leading to eclipses.

questions.q: According to the chapter, on what do day and night depend?
o: Receiving light from the Sun
The Moon going around the Earth
The Earth going around the Sun
The shadow of the Moon falling on the Earth
questions.a: Day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun.

questions.q: The chapter says that, for us to grow, blood has to circulate something from the food all over the body. What?
o: Nutrients
The fibre from the food
The undigested waste from the food
Heat from the Sun
questions.a: The nutrients from the food: to grow, blood has to circulate the nutrients from the food all over the body.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with what the chapter links it to in Column II.
Column I: 1. Eclipses  2. Day and night  3. Telling the time long ago  4. Reading a book at night
Column II: A. Ways we have developed to generate light  B. The Earth and the Moon casting shadows  C. Receiving light from the Sun  D. The position of shadows of objects in the Sun

Read the statements about the chapter.
Statement I: The chapter says our bodies change rapidly, especially around the middle-school years.
Statement II: The chapter says that, over the time life has evolved on Earth, it has found a careless and unbalanced way to get food and breathe.
Statement III: The chapter says light and shadows are useful only for shadow puppets and telling the time.
Which of the statements are correct?
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
questions.a: I only. Statement II is wrong because the chapter says life has figured this out in a beautiful and carefully balanced way; Statement III is wrong because the chapter says light and shadows are NOT just useful for shadow puppets or telling the time.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter treats eclipses as a topic about light and shadows.
Reason (R): The chapter says light and shadows are limited to things around us at home.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the chapter says light and shadows are NOT limited to things around us at home; even the Earth and the Moon cast shadows, leading to eclipses.

questions.q: Sara says, 'To understand eclipses and day and night, it is enough to know how the Earth rotates, how the Moon goes around the Earth and how the Earth goes around the Sun.' According to the chapter, what else do we need to know?
o: The consequences of these movements on life on our planet
How fast the Moon's shadow moves across a classroom wall
How lamps generate light so we can read at night
How shadows are used to make shadow puppets
questions.a: The consequences of these movements on life on our beautiful planet.

questions.q: The chapter says that to understand eclipses and day and night we need to know three movements. Name any two of them.
questions.a: Any two of: the Earth rotates around its axis; the Moon goes around the Earth; the Earth goes around the Sun.
s: One movement named correctly
A second, different movement

questions.q: True or False: The chapter says that only humans have life processes. Give the verdict and correct the statement if needed.
questions.a: False. The chapter says there are life processes essential to all animals for their survival, not just humans.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: life processes are essential to all animals for their survival

questions.q: After saying that a clock or a wrist watch tells us the time, the chapter asks two questions about time. Write both questions.
questions.a: How do we measure time? How fast does something happen?
s: How do we measure time?
How fast does something happen?

questions.q:
Ankit reads a storybook at 10 p.m., long after sunset.
(a) Which idea of the chapter explains how he can do this?
(b) Give one other use of light or shadows that the chapter mentions.
questions.a: (a) We have developed a lot of ways to generate light, so we can read a book at night even when the Sun doesn't shine. (b) Any one of: light helps us see; shadow puppets; telling the time from shadows.
s: (a) we have developed many ways to generate light, so we can read at night
(b) another use: helps us see / shadow puppets / telling the time

questions.q:
Sahil's school shoes stop fitting every few months.
(a) What does the chapter say about our bodies during the middle-school years?
(b) Name two things the chapter says we have to do to grow.
questions.a: (a) Our bodies are changing rapidly, especially around the middle-school years. (b) Any two of: eat; breathe; blood has to circulate the nutrients from the food all over the body.
s: (a) bodies change rapidly in the middle-school years
(b) two of: eat, breathe, blood circulating nutrients

questions.q:
Pari makes the shadow of her hand on a wall with a torch. Her brother says, 'Shadows are only small, at-home things like this; they have nothing to do with the sky.'
(a) What does the chapter say about whether light and shadows are limited to things around us at home?
(b) Give the chapter's example of shadows on a much larger scale, and say what it leads to.
questions.a: (a) Light and shadows are not just limited to things around us at home. (b) Even the Earth and the Moon can cast shadows, which leads to eclipses; so her brother is wrong.
s: (a) light and shadows are not limited to things at home
(b) the Earth and the Moon cast shadows, leading to eclipses

questions.q: The chapter asks questions about plants after describing life processes in animals. Write three of these questions about plants.
questions.a: Any three of: Don't plants also need food to grow? How do they get their food? Do they also breathe? How (do they breathe)?
s: First question about plants
Second question about plants
Third question about plants

questions.q: Explain, in three linked steps, how the chapter connects time, light and the movements of the Earth and the Moon.
questions.a: Step 1: early humans used the position of shadows of objects in the Sun to tell the time, linking time with light and shadows. Step 2: light and shadows are not limited to things at home; the Earth and the Moon cast shadows, causing eclipses, and day and night depend on light from the Sun. Step 3: to understand these we need to know how the Earth rotates around its axis, the Moon goes around the Earth and the Earth goes around the Sun.
s: Time linked to light: early humans told time from shadow positions
Light and shadows on a large scale: eclipses, and day and night from the Sun's light
These need the movements: Earth's rotation, Moon around Earth, Earth around Sun

questions.q: Riya says, 'Light matters to us only because it helps us see. Everything else about light is just for fun, like shadow puppets.' Test her claim against the chapter: give two other things the chapter links to light or shadows, then give your verdict with a third reason.
questions.a: Riya is wrong. First, early humans used the position of the shadows of objects in the Sun to tell the time. Second, day and night depend on receiving light from the Sun. Third, asking questions about the nature of light has given us a very deep understanding of the universe we live in, which is far more than seeing or play.
s: One link: early humans told the time from the position of shadows in the Sun (or day and night depend on light from the Sun)
A second, different link from the same pair
Verdict: the claim is wrong, because questions about the nature of light gave a very deep understanding of the universe

questions.q:
Meghna is making a five-line summary card on the last part of the chapter. Answer each line in one short phrase.
(a) What does the chapter say a clock on the wall or a wrist watch tells us?
(b) In what kind of way does the chapter say life on Earth has figured out how to eat, breathe and grow?

(b) a beautiful and carefully balanced way

questions.q:
A Class 7 group noted the sunrise and sunset times in their town on three days of the year.
1 January: sunrise 7:10 a.m., sunset 5:40 p.m.
1 April: sunrise 6:20 a.m., sunset 6:30 p.m.
1 June: sunrise 5:45 a.m., sunset 7:00 p.m.
(a) Find the length of daytime on each of the three days.
(b) Taking a full day as 24 hours, find the length of the night on 1 January.
(c) Which day had the longest daytime, and by how much was it longer than on 1 January?
(d) Kunal says, 'The change in daytime from 1 January to 1 June is explained by the Earth rotating around its axis alone.' The chapter names three movements we need to know to understand day and night. Using the data, decide whether Kunal is right and justify your decision.
questions.a: (a) 1 January: 10 h 30 min; 1 April: 12 h 10 min; 1 June: 13 h 15 min. (b) 24 h - 10 h 30 min = 13 h 30 min. (c) 1 June, longer by 2 h 45 min. (d) Kunal is not right. The Earth's rotation around its axis gives us day and night every day, but it repeats the same way each day; the data show daytime growing by 2 h 45 min over months, a slow change that the daily spin alone cannot account for. The chapter does not stop at rotation: it says we also need to know how the Earth goes around the Sun (and the Moon around the Earth), so another movement must be considered.
s: (a) 10 h 30 min, 12 h 10 min and 13 h 15 min
(b) night on 1 January is 13 h 30 min
(c) 1 June, longer by 2 h 45 min

(d) decides Kunal is not right: the daily rotation repeats each day, but daytime changed by 2 h 45 min over months, so another movement the chapter names (the Earth going around the Sun) must be considered

questions.q:
An old fort in Rajasthan has a stone sundial: a slanted wall whose shadow falls on hour marks. A Class 7 group compared its readings with a phone clock on one visit.
9:00 a.m. (sunny): sundial read about half past 8.
12:00 noon (sunny): sundial read about half past 11.
3:00 p.m. (thick clouds): no clear shadow, no reading.
7:30 p.m. (after sunset): no shadow, no reading.
(a) Which practice of early humans, described in the chapter, does the sundial use?
(b) On the two sunny checks, by how many minutes was the sundial behind the phone clock, and was the gap the same both times?
(c) Why did it also fail at 3:00 p.m., even though it was still daytime?
(d) The fort can afford only one time display at its gate: a copy of the sundial or an electric clock. Decide which it should choose, and justify using the data.
questions.a: (a) Using the position of the shadows of objects in the Sun to tell the time. (b) At 9:00 it read 8:30 and at 12:00 it read 11:30, so it was 30 minutes behind both times; the gap was the same. (c) Thick clouds blocked the Sun's light, so no clear shadow formed. (d) Either, if justified with the data: the electric clock, because the sundial gave no reading in 2 of the 4 checks (clouds and night) and was about half an hour behind the phone in the other 2; or the sundial, because in sunshine it worked with no electricity and shows visitors how early humans told the time, with a notice that it runs about half an hour behind clock time.
s: (a) telling the time from the position of shadows in the Sun
(b) 30 minutes behind at both sunny checks; the same gap
(c) clouds blocked the sunlight, so no clear shadow
(d) a decision justified with the data (2 of 4 checks gave no reading and the 2 sunny readings were about 30 min behind, or it worked in sunshine)
